background.definition: Infection with dimorphic yeast of Histoplasmosis capsulatum can cause a variable clinical course from asymptomatic self limited infection to progressive infection which may be life threatening.

list.listitem: Eighty percent of people living in endemic areas are skin test positive.
Infection with dimorphic yeast of histoplasmosis capsulatum.
Ohio and Mississippi river valleys are considered endemic areas in United States.

Patients taking TNF-alpha inhibitors should be monitored closely for reactivation of histoplasmosis. The FDA required safety labeling changes to these agents as 240 cases had been reported up to September 2008 with 45 deaths due to histoplasmosis.
Inhalation of spores from disrupted soil, then spread hematogenously to the reticuloendothelial tissues in the first few weeks.

Development of cellular mediated immunity results in spontaneous resolution in 99% of infections. Patients with poor cell-mediated immunity are at high risk for progressive infection. A high volume of inhaled spores may also cause progressive infection.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Exposure to disrupted soil in endemic area

list.listitem: Most important factor is to obtain a travel, work, and social history due to geographic preference of Histoplasmosis.
Spectrum of illness ranges from asymptomatic to severe pneumonia with respiratory failure, depending on the intensity of exposure, and the immunity of the host.
Nonspecific symptoms of cough, fever, sputum production, weight loss, and occasional chest discomfort. Histoplasmosis can mimic lung cancer.
Of symptomatic infections, 60% are acute pulmonary, 10% each are chronic pulmonary, pericarditis, rheumatologic, or disseminated, and less than 1% are fibrosing mediastinitis.
Diagnostic testing depends on clinical syndrome of infection.
Gold standard is culture of H. capsulatum in sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, blood, or tissue specimens. However, cultures may take up to 6 weeks to show growth.

Serologic testing includes both complement fixation (CF) and immunodiffusion (ID). CF is more sensitive but less specific than ID. Serologic tests are not useful in immunocompromised patients who cannot mount a response to infection.
Consider bronchoscopy for moderate to severe cases with radiographic changes for histopathologic diagnosis.
The best use of the urinary antigen is in AIDS patients with disseminated histoplasmosis.
There was 98% agreement between paired urine and serum histoplasmosis antigen tests from the same patient and completed within a week of each other among 601 paired samples.
Skin testing reagents are no longer available in the United States.
Evidence of bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia) and hepatocellular enzyme elevations may be found in disseminated histoplasmosis.
At MD Anderson Cancer Center, the most common identified etiology of previously undiagnosed pulmonary lesions was histoplasmosis (41% 12/29) following open-lung biopsy.
See for an overview of diagnostic testing.

Among a pediatric population presenting with mediastinal massees in a histoplasmosis endemic area, the presence of the combination of lymphopenia, anterior mediastinal mass location, or enlarged cervical lymph nodes on CT scanning had a positive predictive value of 86% and a negative predictive value of 97% for cancer.

In patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodulce (IPN) in areas endemic for histoplasmosis, the positive predictive value of positivity for both IgG and IgM antibodies (at acute infection levels) was 100% for benign disease (i.e., no cancer).
The vast majority of patients have asymptomatic self limited infections; only 1% of infected patients will have a clinically significant manifestation.
Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion based upon risks for deficits in cell-mediated immunity (e.g. AIDS, TNF-alpha blockers) and travel to or residing in endemic areas.
Patients with cell-mediated immunity are at a higher risk for progressive infection.
Treatment is indicated in moderate to severe acute pulmonary histoplasmosis, chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis, disseminated histoplasmosis, and CNS histoplasmosis (). A
The efficacy of treatment for mediastinal granuloma or lymphadenitis and mild acute focal pulmonary infection is unknown (). C
Mild cases are usually self limited and do not require therapy.

Treatment is indicated in moderate to severe acute pulmonary histoplasmosis, chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis, disseminated histoplasmosis, CNS histoplasmosis. The efficacy of treatment for mediastinal granuloma or lymphadenitis and mild acute focal pulmonary infection is unknown. See for specific treatment recommendations.
Itraconazole levels should be monitored; it is a strong CYP3A4 enzyme inhibitor. The oral suspension of itraconazole has a higher bioavailability than the capsules.
In cases of fibrosing mediastinitis, surgery should be avoided.
Rare case reports of stenting of great vessels and/or airways with fibrosing mediastinitis have been published, but this is generally not indicated.
Patients with signs of SIRS or respiratory distress should be hospitalized.
Majority of exposures result in asymptomatic infections. C
Acute pulmonary infections are also commonly self limited. C
Lipid formulation amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg daily for 4-6 weeks) is recommended for treatment.
Azole drugs are not safe in pregnancy.
Consider inspecting placenta for granulomas as evidence for possible transmission to baby and monitor baby for infections.
Treatment indications are the same for adults except that amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg daily) is usually well tolerated and lipid formulations are not preferred.
Itraconazole dosing in children is 5 to 10 mg/kg/divided in 2 daily doses; avoid the suspension.
